claims.statement: According to the Kojiki, Susanoo is a kami who emerged from Izanagi’s nose during purification after a visit to Yomi.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Kojiki, Susanoo adalah kami yang muncul dari hidung Izanagi ketika ia menyucikan diri sesudah mengunjungi Yomi.
claims.quote: A kami introduced by (Kojiki) as having come into being from the nose of Izanagi no mikoto as he was performing ablutions (misogi) to rid himself of pollution encountered while in the underworld (Yomi).

claims.statement: The stories of Izumo feature in Japan’s early myths.
claims.statement_id: Kisah Izumo termasuk mitos awal Jepang.
claims.quote: The Izumo region and Izumo Oyashiro Shrine feature prominently in several of Japan’s earliest myths.

claims.statement: The Nihongi says Susanoo was born to Izanagi and Izanami.
claims.statement_id: Nihongi menyebut Susanoo lahir dari Izanagi dan Izanami.
claims.quote: In Nihongi, however, Susanoo is described as being produced by Izanagi and Izanami

claims.statement: Both accounts place Susanoo with Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi among the three noble children.
claims.statement_id: Kedua sumber menempatkan Susanoo bersama Amaterasu dan Tsukuyomi sebagai tiga anak mulia.
claims.quote: Both accounts describe Susanoo as one of a set of three kami known as the "three noble children," the other being Amaterasu and Tsukuyomi

claims.statement: Susanoo has been associated with wind and rain.
claims.statement_id: Susanoo dikaitkan dengan angin dan hujan.
claims.quote: Susanoo has been associated with wind and rain, but many elements of his personality remain unclear.

claims.statement: Susanoo was banished after causing Amaterasu to hide in the heavenly cave.
claims.statement_id: Susanoo diusir setelah menyebabkan Amaterasu bersembunyi di gua langit.
claims.quote: Susanoo ran amok and caused Amaterasu to hide herself away in the heavenly cave, for which offense Susanoo was again banished.

claims.statement: Susanoo defeated Yamata no Orochi and received the sword Kusanagi.
claims.statement_id: Susanoo mengalahkan Yamata no Orochi dan memperoleh pedang Kusanagi.
claims.quote: Susanoo defeated the serpent Yamata no orochi, received the sword "Kusanagi"

claims.statement: Susanoo agreed to slay the serpent in exchange for marrying the couple’s daughter.
claims.statement_id: Susanoo setuju membunuh ular itu agar dapat menikahi putri pasangan tersebut.
claims.quote: Susanoo agreed to slay the beast in exchange for permission to marry their daughter.

claims.statement: Izanagi is a primordial Shinto god believed to have helped create the islands of Japan.
claims.statement_id: Izanagi adalah dewa purba Shinto yang dipercaya ikut menciptakan pulau-pulau Jepang.
claims.quote: Izanami ('she who invites') and Izanagi ('he who invites') are the primordial gods of the Shinto religion who are believed to have created the islands of Japan

claims.statement: According to the Kojiki and Nihongi, Izanagi and Izanami are central to the world’s formation.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Kojiki dan Nihongi, Izanagi bersama Izanami berperan utama dalam pembentukan dunia.
claims.quote: According to Kojiki and Nihongi, one of the two kami (together with his consort Izanami) principally responsible for the formation of the world.

claims.statement: The two kami stand on a heavenly bridge and stir the sea with a spear; its drips form Onogoro Island.
claims.statement_id: Kedua kami berdiri di jembatan langit dan mengaduk laut dengan tombak; tetesannya menjadi Pulau Onogoro.
claims.quote: According to the myth, the two kami first stood on the "floating bridge of heaven" and used a spear to stir the sea below, whereupon the brine dripping from the spear's point congealed and formed the island of Onogoro.

claims.statement: Izanami died as a result of giving birth to the fire kami.
claims.statement_id: Izanami meninggal akibat melahirkan dewa api.
claims.quote: Izanami died as the result of giving birth to the kami of fire

claims.statement: Izanagi followed Izanami to Yomi.
claims.statement_id: Izanagi mengikuti Izanami ke Yomi.
claims.quote: Izanagi, no doubt unable to live without his beloved wife, rashly followed her down into the underworld or Yomi

claims.statement: Izanagi sealed Yomi with a large stone and performed river purification.
claims.statement_id: Izanagi menutup pintu Yomi dengan batu besar dan menjalani penyucian diri di sungai.
claims.quote: On finally reaching the outside world, Izanagi blocked the entrance to Yomi with an enormous stone. Fortunate to escape unharmed from such a terrible place of darkness the god had to perform a cleansing ritual in the river Woto to rid himself of the impurities of the underworld.

claims.statement: During purification, Amaterasu emerges from his left eye, Tsuki-yomi from his right, and Susanoo from his nose.
claims.statement_id: Saat penyucian, Amaterasu lahir dari mata kiri, Tsuki-yomi dari mata kanan, dan Susanoo dari hidung Izanagi.
claims.quote: It was during these rituals that various gods were born: Amaterasu, the sun goddess, when he washed his left eye, Tsuki-yomi, the god of the moon, when he washed his right eye, Susanoo (or Take-haya-Susa-no-wo), the storm god, when he washed his nose

claims.statement: Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, and Susanoo are known as the three noble children.
claims.statement_id: Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, dan Susanoo dikenal sebagai tiga anak mulia.
claims.quote: the "three noble children" Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, and Susanoo were also produced at this time

claims.statement: Yōkai are supernatural beings and phenomena of Japanese folklore, including spirits and monsters.
claims.statement_id: Yōkai adalah makhluk dan gejala gaib dalam cerita rakyat Jepang, termasuk roh dan monster.
claims.quote: Yōkai (妖怪) are creatures and phenomena of Japanese folklore including spirits, monsters, and just about all things supernatural.

claims.statement: In Japanese folklore, yōkai includes legendary ghosts, monsters, and spirits.
claims.statement_id: Dalam cerita rakyat Jepang, yōkai mencakup hantu, monster, dan roh legendaris.
claims.quote: In Japanese folklore, yōkai (妖怪) refers to legendary ghosts, monsters, and spirits.

claims.statement: Yōkai is a broad term with no precise English equivalent.
claims.statement_id: Yōkai adalah istilah luas yang tidak memiliki padanan bahasa Inggris yang tepat.
claims.quote: it is a broad and vague term with no real English translation

claims.statement: Yōkai may be depicted as humans with altered features, animals, plants, insects, or household objects.
claims.statement_id: Yōkai dapat digambarkan menyerupai manusia berciri berubah, binatang, tumbuhan, serangga, atau benda rumah tangga.
claims.quote: some resembling humans, for example, with altered features such as a long neck or three eyes. Others looked like strange animals, plants, insects, or household goods.

claims.statement: Yōkai culture appears in picture scrolls and multicolored woodblock prints.
claims.statement_id: Budaya yōkai hadir dalam gulungan gambar dan cetakan kayu berwarna.
claims.quote: This exhibition introduces Japan’s yokai (Japanese folkloric imaginary monsters) culture that extends to the present day through picture scrolls and nishiki-e (a multicolored Japanese woodblock print)

claims.statement: Yōkai, once feared, have also come to be viewed as friendlier presences.
claims.statement_id: Yōkai yang dahulu ditakuti juga kemudian dilihat sebagai sosok yang lebih ramah.
claims.quote: yokai seem to have gradually become less of a subject of fear and have come to be viewed as a more charming and friendly presence.

claims.statement: Yōkai appear in media including toys and films.
claims.statement_id: Yōkai hadir dalam media seperti mainan dan film.
claims.quote: as well as a diverse range of media, including toys and films.

claims.statement: Tsukuyomi is a male kami regarded as ruling over the night.
claims.statement_id: Tsukuyomi adalah kami laki-laki yang dianggap berkuasa atas malam.
claims.quote: The second of Izanagi and Izanami's "three noble children," and usually considered a male kami with rule over the night.

claims.statement: Tsukuyomi is a moon kami in Japanese mythology and Shinto.
claims.statement_id: Tsukuyomi adalah kami bulan dalam mitologi Jepang dan agama Shinto.
claims.quote: moon kami in Japanese mythology and the Shinto religion.

claims.statement: Tsukuyomi’s name is thought to relate to reading moon phases in the lunar calendar.
claims.statement_id: Nama Tsukuyomi diduga berkaitan dengan pembacaan fase bulan dalam kalender lunar.
claims.quote: The name tsuku-yomi is thought to be originally related to the lunar calendar, and refers to the "reading" (yomu) of the phases of the "moon" (tsuki).

claims.statement: According to the Kojiki and one Nihongi version, Tsukuyomi emerged when Izanagi washed his right eye.
claims.statement_id: Menurut Kojiki dan versi Nihongi, Tsukuyomi muncul saat Izanagi membasuh mata kanannya.
claims.quote: According to Kojiki and an "alternate writing" in Nihongi, Tsukuyomi came into being when Izanagi washed his right eye as he was undergoing ablution.

claims.statement: The Nihongi gives Tsukuyomi the sea, while the Kojiki gives him the night.
claims.statement_id: Nihongi menempatkan Tsukuyomi atas laut, sedangkan Kojiki atas malam.
claims.quote: Tsukuyomi was entrusted by Izanagi with rule variously over the sea (Nihongi) or over the realm of night (Kojiki).

claims.statement: A Nihongi version says Tsukuyomi killed Ukemochi and was separated from the sun by Amaterasu, explaining day and night.
claims.statement_id: Versi Nihongi menyatakan Tsukuyomi membunuh Ukemochi lalu dipisahkan dari matahari oleh Amaterasu, menjelaskan pemisahan siang dan malam.
claims.quote: an "alternate writing" in Nihongi relates that Tsukuyomi originally resided together with Amaterasu in heaven, but after killing the kami of foods Ukemochi, he was condemned by Amaterasu as an "evil kami" and forced to live apart from the sun, resulting in the separation of day and night.

claims.statement: Tsukuyomi is worshiped at Tsukuyomi no Miya in Ise.
claims.statement_id: Tsukuyomi dipuja di Tsukuyomi no Miya di Ise.
claims.quote: Tsukuyomi is the object of worship (saijin) at the detached shrine (betsugū) Tsukuyomi no Miya of the Grand Shrines of Ise

claims.statement: Tsukuyomi is enshrined at Tsukiyomi-no-miya and associated with the moon.
claims.statement_id: Tsukuyomi dipuja di Tsukiyomi-no-miya dan dikaitkan dengan bulan.
claims.quote: Tsukiyomi-no-Mikoto is the deity of Tsukiyomi-no-miya / the Koutaijingu Betsugu.It is a younger brother of Amaterasu Omikami and is likened to the moon.

claims.statement: Tengu can be considered yōkai or kami.
claims.statement_id: Tengu dapat dianggap sebagai yōkai atau kami.
claims.quote: They are considered a type of yōkai (supernatural being) or kami (god or spirit).

claims.statement: In Japanese folk belief, tengu inhabit high mountain woodlands.
claims.statement_id: Menurut kepercayaan rakyat Jepang, tengu menghuni hutan pegunungan tinggi.
claims.quote: a tengu, the embodiment of powerful and usually malevolent spirits who, in Japanese folk beliefs, inhabit the woodlands of high mountains.

claims.statement: Tengu are usually portrayed with human bodies, wings, and sometimes talons.
claims.statement_id: Tengu biasanya digambarkan bertubuh manusia, bersayap, dan kadang bercakar.
claims.quote: They are typically represented as having human bodies, wings, and sometimes talons in place of hands and feet.

claims.statement: Karasu Tengu has a birdlike head and sharp beak; Ko no ha Tengu has a human face and very long nose.
claims.statement_id: Karasu Tengu berkepala burung berparuh tajam, sedangkan Ko no ha Tengu berwajah manusia berhidung sangat panjang.
claims.quote: The Karasu Tengu has a birdlike head complete with a strong, sharp beak. The Ko no ha Tengu has a human face, distorted by an enormously long nose.

claims.statement: Tengu are credited with great strength, flight, shape-changing, and possessing humans.
claims.statement_id: Tengu dikisahkan memiliki kekuatan luar biasa, terbang, berubah wujud, dan merasuki manusia.
claims.quote: They are credited with many powers, including supernatural strength and the ability to fly, to assume other forms, and to take over humans through possession.

claims.statement: Tengu are sometimes described as benevolent spirits protecting people or temples.
claims.statement_id: Tengu kadang digambarkan sebagai roh baik yang melindungi orang atau kuil.
claims.quote: Occasionally, however, tengu appear as benevolent spirits who protect certain individuals or temples.

claims.statement: Older tales portray tengu as enemies of Buddhism who trick priests or burn temples.
claims.statement_id: Kisah lama menggambarkan tengu sebagai musuh agama Buddha yang menipu pendeta atau membakar kuil.
claims.quote: portray tengu as enemies of Buddhism, setting fires at temples or tricking priests.

claims.statement: Tengu’s image changed; by the Edo period they were also enlisted to help find missing children.
claims.statement_id: Citra tengu berubah; pada zaman Edo mereka juga diminta membantu mencari anak hilang.
claims.quote: For instance, tengu were long thought to abduct children, but by the Edo period they often were enlisted to aid in the search for missing children.

claims.statement: Inari is a tutelary deity of rice cultivation and the five grains.
claims.statement_id: Inari adalah dewa pelindung budidaya padi dan lima jenis biji-bijian.
claims.quote: A tutelary deity of rice cultivation and the five grains.

claims.statement: People throughout Japan pray to Inari Okami.
claims.statement_id: Orang di seluruh Jepang berdoa kepada Inari Okami.
claims.quote: People throughout Japan pray to Inari Okami for these things

claims.statement: Shinto classics call Inari Uka-no-mitama-no-kami.
claims.statement_id: Kitab-kitab Shinto menyebut Inari Uka-no-mitama-no-kami.
claims.quote: In the Shinto classics Inari is desiguated as Uka-no-mitama-no-kami.

claims.statement: Five enshrined deities at Fushimi Inari Taisha embody virtues of Inari Okami.
claims.statement_id: Lima tempat pemujaan utama Fushimi Inari Taisha mewakili keutamaan Inari Okami.
claims.quote: These five pillars of Fushimi Inari Taisha are named for the great virtues of Inari Okami that they embody.

claims.statement: Inari belief has a close association with foxes.
claims.statement_id: Kepercayaan Inari berhubungan erat dengan rubah.
claims.quote: Inari faith also has a deep association with foxes.

claims.statement: In commercial regions Inari was linked to prosperity, and in fishing villages to fishing.
claims.statement_id: Di daerah perdagangan, Inari dipercaya membawa kemakmuran usaha; di desa nelayan ia dikaitkan dengan perikanan.
claims.quote: In commercial regions, Inari was believed to be the kami who ensured commercial prosperity. In fishing villages Inari was the kami of fishing.

claims.statement: Fushimi Inari Shrine connects the name Inari with an older expression for reaping rice.
claims.statement_id: Kuil Fushimi Inari mengaitkan nama Inari dengan ungkapan lama tentang panen padi.
claims.quote: “Inari” is short for “Ine nari” or “Ine ni naru” (reaping of rice).

claims.statement: Izanami is a kami who bore deities of the land and is associated with an earth-mother image.
claims.statement_id: Izanami adalah kami yang melahirkan dewa-dewa alam dan dikaitkan dengan citra ibu bumi.
claims.quote: As the kami responsible for the birth of various other kami representing the land and its contents, Izanami has strong connotations of an "earth mother" goddess.

claims.statement: Izanami and Izanagi are believed to have created Japan’s islands and given birth to many Shinto gods.
claims.statement_id: Izanami dan Izanagi dipercaya menciptakan pulau-pulau Jepang dan melahirkan banyak dewa Shinto.
claims.quote: Izanami ('she who invites') and Izanagi ('he who invites') are the primordial gods of the Shinto religion who are believed to have created the islands of Japan and given birth to many of the other Shinto gods or kami.

claims.statement: Izanami is Izanagi’s consort.
claims.statement_id: Izanami adalah pasangan Izanagi.
claims.quote: Consort of the kami Izanagi. The name Izanami has been understood in various ways

claims.statement: Izanami was burned giving birth to the fire god, then fell ill and died.
claims.statement_id: Izanami terbakar saat melahirkan dewa api, lalu sakit dan meninggal.
claims.quote: Burning her genitals as she gave birth to the god of fire, Izanami fell sick and then died

claims.statement: Izanagi followed Izanami to Yomi.
claims.statement_id: Izanagi menyusul Izanami ke Yomi.
claims.quote: Izanagi, no doubt unable to live without his beloved wife, rashly followed her down into the underworld or Yomi

claims.statement: Izanagi was shocked by Izanami’s decayed appearance and fled.
claims.statement_id: Izanagi terkejut melihat wujud Izanami yang membusuk, lalu melarikan diri.
claims.quote: was shocked by the putrefying appearance of his dead wife, whereupon he fled from the place

claims.statement: Izanami threatened to kill one thousand people daily, and Izanagi replied he would give birth to fifteen hundred.
claims.statement_id: Izanami mengancam akan membunuh seribu orang setiap hari, dan Izanagi menjawab akan melahirkan seribu lima ratus orang.
claims.quote: the dead Izanami threatened to kill one thousand persons each day, but Izanagi stated that he would respond by giving birth to fifteen hundred persons

claims.statement: Yuki-onna is a Japanese yōkai without a single definitive story.
claims.statement_id: Yuki-onna adalah yōkai Jepang yang tidak mempunyai satu kisah tunggal.
claims.quote: The Yuki Onna is one of Japan’s most well-known and yet unknown yokai. There is no single story of the Yuki Onna.

claims.statement: The name Yuki-onna means snow woman.
claims.statement_id: Nama Yuki-onna berarti perempuan salju.
claims.quote: Yuki Onna uses the kanji 雪 (yuki; snow) + 女 (onna; woman) to mean Snow Woman.

claims.statement: Yuki-onna stories occur in snowy parts of Japan and have regional variants.
claims.statement_id: Cerita Yuki-onna terdapat di daerah Jepang yang bersalju dan memiliki variasi daerah.
claims.quote: Anywhere there is ice and snow in Japan you will find legends of the Yuki Onna, often called by some regional variation.

claims.statement: Yuki-onna is often depicted with white skin and a white kimono.
claims.statement_id: Yuki-onna kerap digambarkan berkulit putih dan mengenakan kimono putih.
claims.quote: She resembles a classic yurei, with snow-white skin and a white kimono. The kimono is usually described as a thin, summer kimono

claims.statement: In Hearn’s story, a woman in white blows her breath on Mosaku.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah Hearn, seorang perempuan berbaju putih meniupkan napasnya ke Mosaku.
claims.quote: he saw a woman in the room,—a woman all in white. She was bending above Mosaku, and blowing her breath upon him

claims.statement: The woman spares Minokichi because he is young.
claims.statement_id: Perempuan itu membiarkan Minokichi hidup karena usianya muda.
claims.quote: But I cannot help feeling some pity for you,—because you are so young... You are a pretty boy, Minokichi; and I will not hurt you now.

claims.statement: The woman forbids Minokichi from telling anyone and threatens to kill him if he does.
claims.statement_id: Perempuan itu melarang Minokichi bercerita kepada siapa pun dan mengancam akan membunuhnya jika ia melanggar.
claims.quote: But, if you ever tell anybody—even your own mother—about what you have seen this night, I shall know it; and then I will kill you

claims.statement: O-Yuki reveals she was the snow woman Minokichi met.
claims.statement_id: O-Yuki mengaku sebagai perempuan salju yang ditemui Minokichi.
claims.quote: “It was I—I—I! Yuki it was! And I told you then that I would kill you if you ever said one word about it!

claims.statement: Kappa is an amphibious supernatural being and water spirit in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Kappa adalah makhluk amfibi gaib dan roh air dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: Kappa (河童 river-child) is an amphibious supernatural monster and water spirit in Japanese folklore.

claims.statement: Kappa are among Japan’s well-known yōkai.
claims.statement_id: Kappa termasuk yōkai terkenal di Jepang.
claims.quote: Kappa are among Japan’s most famous yōkai.

claims.statement: A contemporary Japanese image shows kappa with green childlike bodies and round head dishes.
claims.statement_id: Gambaran Jepang masa kini menampilkan kappa bertubuh hijau seperti anak dan memiliki cekungan bundar di kepala.
claims.quote: Contemporary Japanese people typically visualize kappa as having green, hairless bodies shaped like that of a human child. They have smooth, circular dishes on their heads

claims.statement: Kappa are said to live in rivers and ponds and drag swimmers into the water.
claims.statement_id: Kappa dikisahkan tinggal di sungai dan kolam serta menyeret perenang ke air.
claims.quote: Kappa live in rivers and ponds, where they catch hold of the feet of swimmers, dragging them to a watery death.

claims.statement: Before the eighteenth century kappa were also seen as monkeylike or otterlike.
claims.statement_id: Sebelum abad kedelapan belas kappa juga dipandang menyerupai monyet atau berang-berang.
claims.quote: Kappa were also thought of as mammals like monkeys or otters until the eighteenth century, rather than reptiles or amphibians.

claims.statement: From the 1950s kappa were also portrayed as cute.
claims.statement_id: Sejak 1950-an kappa juga digambarkan sebagai makhluk lucu.
claims.quote: it was not until the 1950s that the creatures were portrayed as straightforwardly cute.

claims.statement: Contemporary depictions show birdlike beaks and turtlelike shells.
claims.statement_id: Gambaran masa kini menunjukkan paruh burung dan tempurung mirip kura-kura.
claims.quote: pointed beaks like birds, which are often yellow. On their backs, they have what looks like a turtle’s shell

claims.statement: Kappa are said to enjoy sumō but may harm defeated opponents.
claims.statement_id: Kappa dikisahkan gemar sumo namun dapat mencelakai lawan yang kalah.
claims.quote: In folklore, kappa are commonly said to enjoy sumō, and this may seem superficially charming, but not if they pull defeated humans beneath the water, or otherwise harm them.

claims.statement: Uzume is the goddess whose dance drew Amaterasu from the heavenly rock cave.
claims.statement_id: Uzume adalah dewi yang menari untuk menarik Amaterasu keluar dari gua langit.
claims.quote: The goddess who danced so as to lure Amaterasu from the heavenly rock cave.

claims.statement: In Japanese mythology, Uzume’s dance to draw out Amaterasu is linked with kagura’s origin.
claims.statement_id: Dalam mitologi Jepang, tari Uzume yang memanggil Amaterasu dikaitkan dengan asal kagura.
claims.quote: According to Japanese mythology, the origins of kagura lie with a dance performed by the Goddess Ame-no-uzume-no-mikoto to bring out Amaterasu Oomikami

claims.statement: The Kojiki and Nihongi say Uzume experienced divine possession after Amaterasu hid.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki dan Nihongi menyebut Uzume mengalami kerasukan ilahi setelah Amaterasu bersembunyi.
claims.quote: Both Nihongi and Kojiki relate that after Amaterasu hid away in the rock cave of heaven, Amenouzume underwent divine possession (kamigakari)

claims.statement: Uzume’s actions made the kami laugh and drew Amaterasu out of the cave in curiosity.
claims.statement_id: Tindakan Uzume membuat para kami tertawa dan membangkitkan rasa ingin tahu Amaterasu hingga ia keluar dari gua.
claims.quote: This behavior drew amused exclamations from the other assembled kami, and attracted the curiosity of Amaterasu, who at last came out from the cave.

claims.statement: Uzume is regarded as a patron of performing arts and a negotiator with unfamiliar beings.
claims.statement_id: Uzume dipandang sebagai pelindung seni pertunjukan dan perunding dengan makhluk yang belum dikenal.
claims.quote: In addition to her role as patron kami of actors and other performing arts, Uzume is also viewed as having the role of negotiator with new, unknown beings.

claims.statement: Uzume was sent to meet and identify Sarutahiko.
claims.statement_id: Uzume diutus untuk menemui dan mengenali Sarutahiko.
claims.quote: sent her to confront and ascertain the identity of the kami Sarutahiko

claims.statement: Ota Shrine is dedicated to Ame no Uzume.
claims.statement_id: Kuil Ota didedikasikan kepada Ame no Uzume.
claims.quote: Ota Jinja Shrine is located approximately 800 meters to the east of Kamigamo Jinja grounds and is dedicated to Ame no Uzume no Mikoto

claims.statement: Ame no Uzume is worshiped as a deity associated with artistic skill.
claims.statement_id: Ame no Uzume dipuja sebagai dewi yang membantu keterampilan seni.
claims.quote: Ame no Uzume no Mikoto is primarily worshipped as a deity that helps improve artistic skills.

claims.statement: Hachiman is one of the principal Shinto kami.
claims.statement_id: Hachiman adalah salah satu kami utama dalam Shinto.
claims.quote: Hachiman, one of the principal Shintō deities (kami)

claims.statement: The military class historically worshiped Hachiman as a war deity in Japan.
claims.statement_id: Kaum militer memuja Hachiman sebagai dewa perang di Jepang.
claims.quote: Historically worshiped by the military class as a god of war, Hachiman is now the object of deep devotion for many people in Japan.

claims.statement: Hachiman is associated with deified Emperor Ōjin, Jingū, and Himegami, first enshrined at Usa Hachimangū and later at many Japanese shrines.
claims.statement_id: Hachiman berkaitan dengan Kaisar Ōjin yang didewakan bersama Jingū dan Himegami; mereka mula-mula dipuja di Usa Hachimangū lalu di banyak kuil Jepang.
claims.quote: Generally refers to the deified Emperor Ôjin together with his mother Empress Jingû and his wife Himegami. They were first enshrined in the Usa Hachimangû in Oita Prefecture and later in many Hachiman shrines throughout Japan.

claims.statement: Hachiman was among the early indigenous gods assimilated into the Buddhist pantheon in Japan.
claims.statement_id: Hachiman termasuk dewa lokal awal yang dimasukkan ke dalam lingkungan Buddha di Jepang.
claims.quote: was among the first indigenous gods assimilated into the Buddhist pantheon in Japan.

claims.statement: Hachiman received the Buddhist title Daibosatsu.
claims.statement_id: Hachiman memperoleh gelar Buddha Daibosatsu.
claims.quote: By the late eighth century he was officially accorded the Buddhist title Daibosatsu (Great Bodhisattva).

claims.statement: Hachiman was a particular patron of the Minamoto clan.
claims.statement_id: Hachiman adalah pelindung khusus klan Minamoto.
claims.quote: as the particular patron of the Minamoto clan, founders of the first shogunate

claims.statement: Hachiman was regarded as protector of the state in conflict and personal protector of samurai.
claims.statement_id: Hachiman dianggap pelindung negara saat konflik dan pelindung pribadi para samurai.
claims.quote: Hachiman was considered the protector of the state in times of strife and was revered as a personal protector by individual samurai of all ranks.

claims.statement: Yūrei is the spirit of a deceased person.
claims.statement_id: Yūrei adalah roh seseorang yang sudah meninggal.
claims.quote: Generally speaking, a yūrei is the spirit of a person who has died, usually appearing as they did in life.

claims.statement: The meaning of the Japanese word yūrei changed over the centuries.
claims.statement_id: Makna kata yūrei dalam bahasa Jepang berubah selama berabad-abad.
claims.quote: The Japanese word yūrei conjures up an image today of a spiteful ghost, but its meaning has changed considerably over the centuries.

claims.statement: Yūrei may remain in the human world for personal reasons or insufficient funeral rites.
claims.statement_id: Yūrei dapat tinggal di dunia manusia karena alasan pribadi atau upacara pemakaman yang kurang memadai.
claims.quote: Yūrei refers to the spirits of humans who do not cross over to the other side and remain in the human world for personal reasons or because the funeral or burial rites were not sufficient or satisfactory.

claims.statement: In art and literature yūrei are often shown as long-haired women in burial clothes, with dangling hands and no feet.
claims.statement_id: Dalam seni dan sastra, yūrei lazim digambarkan sebagai perempuan berambut hitam panjang, berpakaian pemakaman, bertangan menggantung, dan tanpa kaki.
claims.quote: The typical yūrei, as depicted in art and literature, is described as a woman with long, disheveled black hair obstructing the face, wearing burial clothing, with curved dangling hands and no feet.

claims.statement: In ancient and medieval Japan, yūrei usually meant souls of the dead who neither appeared nor cursed.
claims.statement_id: Di Jepang kuno dan pertengahan, yūrei biasanya berarti jiwa orang mati yang tidak menampakkan diri atau mengutuk.
claims.quote: In ancient and medieval Japan, when there was considerable “commerce” between the people of this world and spirits, the word yūrei typically referred to the souls of the dead, who neither showed themselves nor enacted curses.

claims.statement: Around the fifteenth century, yūrei began to mean resentful spirits.
claims.statement_id: Sekitar abad kelima belas, yūrei mulai berarti roh yang menyimpan dendam.
claims.quote: Around the fifteenth century, the word yūrei began to shift from describing the souls of the memorialized dead to represent spirits harboring a grudge.

claims.statement: In the Edo period, people believed a bad relationship in life could lead to revenge after death.
claims.statement_id: Pada zaman Edo, hubungan buruk semasa hidup dipercaya dapat berujung pada pembalasan setelah kematian.
claims.quote: In the Edo period (1603–1868), there was a belief that a bad relationship with someone in life could lead to that person taking revenge after death.

claims.statement: In the later Edo period, yūrei appeared in kabuki and inspired ukiyo-e artists.
claims.statement_id: Pada akhir zaman Edo, yūrei kerap muncul dalam kabuki dan mengilhami seniman ukiyo-e.
claims.quote: In the later Edo period, it was common for yūrei to appear in kabuki, providing inspiration for ukiyo-e artists.

claims.statement: In the Edo period, ghost stories became popular and artists painted yūrei.
claims.statement_id: Pada zaman Edo, cerita hantu menjadi populer dan seniman melukis yūrei.
claims.quote: there was a craze for kaidan (ghost stories) and many artists painted pictures of yūrei.

claims.statement: Benzaiten derives from the Indian water goddess Sarasvatī and in Japan is a patron of music and eloquence.
claims.statement_id: Benzaiten berasal dari Sarasvatī, dewi air India, dan di Jepang melindungi musik serta kefasihan.
claims.quote: Benzaiten was originally the Indian goddess of water, Sarasvatī, and is known in Japan as a patron tutelary of music and eloquence (wisdom).

claims.statement: Benzaiten derives from Saraswati and was adopted into Shinto and Buddhist pantheons.
claims.statement_id: Benzaiten berasal dari Saraswati dan masuk dalam tradisi Shinto serta Buddha.
claims.quote: Benzaiten originated from the Hindu goddess Saraswati, and has been adopted into the pantheons of both Shinto and Buddhism.

claims.statement: Benzaiten is among the Seven Gods of Good Fortune.
claims.statement_id: Benzaiten termasuk tujuh dewa keberuntungan di Jepang.
claims.quote: "Seven deities of good fortune," seven deities reputed to bring good luck. Most commonly, the seven include Ebisu, Daikoku, Bishamonten, Fukurokuju, Jurōjin, Benzaiten, and Hōtei

claims.statement: The grouping of seven fortune deities is believed to have begun in Japan’s Muromachi period.
claims.statement_id: Kelompok tujuh dewa keberuntungan diyakini bermula pada masa Muromachi di Jepang.
claims.quote: The cult of seven deities of good fortune is believed to have originated in Japan's Muromachi period

claims.statement: Ugajin merged with Benzaiten as Uga Benten.
claims.statement_id: Ugajin berpadu dengan Benzaiten menjadi Uga Benten.
claims.quote: Fused with the Buddhist deity Benzaiten, the kami became known as Uga Benten

claims.statement: Uga Benten is portrayed as a heavenly woman with eight arms.
claims.statement_id: Bentuk Uga Benten digambarkan sebagai perempuan langit berlengan delapan.
claims.quote: Their contents depict the deity in the form of a heavenly woman with eight arms

claims.statement: A white snake with an elderly human face rests on her head.
claims.statement_id: Seekor ular putih berkepala manusia tua berada di kepalanya.
claims.quote: A white snake with the face of an elderly human rests on her head

claims.statement: Uga Benten differs from other sutra depictions; worship spread from Chikubujima to Itsukushima, Enoshima, and Tenkawa.
claims.statement_id: Gambaran Uga Benten berbeda dari sutra lain; pemujaannya menyebar dari Chikubujima ke Itsukushima, Enoshima, dan Tenkawa.
claims.quote: These depictions differ greatly from the conventional portrait of Benzaiten found in the sutras Dainichikyō and Saishōō-kyō, and reflect a unique development of the Benten cult in Japan. From Ōmi Chikubujima near Mt. Hiei, the cult of Uga Benzaiten spread throughout Japan, including Itsukushima in Aki, Enoshima in Sagami, and Tenkawa in Kii

claims.statement: Yamata no Orochi is a great serpent whose name means eight-forked snake.
claims.statement_id: Yamata no Orochi ialah ular besar yang namanya berarti ular bercabang delapan.
claims.quote: A great serpent (the name means "eight-forked-snake")

claims.statement: Yamata no Orochi is a mythological monster of Japan described in the Kojiki as an eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent.
claims.statement_id: Yamata no Orochi adalah monster mitos Jepang yang digambarkan dalam Kojiki sebagai ular berkepala dan berekor delapan.
claims.quote: The Yamata-no-Orochi is perhaps the most frightening of all Japan’s many mythological monsters. According to the Kojiki, this fearsome serpent had eight heads and eight tails

claims.statement: The serpent has eight heads and tails, red eyes, and spans eight peaks and valleys.
claims.statement_id: Ular itu berkepala dan berekor delapan, bermata merah, dan membentang melintasi delapan gunung serta lembah.
claims.quote: a huge snake, with eight heads and eight tails, eyes red like a Chinese lantern plant, and a length that spanned eight peaks and eight valleys.

claims.statement: Orochi ate the couple’s other daughters and would return for Kushinada-hime.
claims.statement_id: Orochi memakan putri-putri pasangan itu dan akan kembali untuk Kushinada-hime.
claims.quote: an eight-headed, eight-tailed serpent known as the Yamata no Orochi had eaten all their other daughters and would shortly return for Kushinada-hime.

claims.statement: Susanoo made the serpent drunk on rice wine and killed it.
claims.statement_id: Susanoo membuat ular itu mabuk dengan arak beras lalu membunuhnya.
claims.quote: Susanoo made the serpent drunk on rice wine and then killed it.

claims.statement: Susanoo found Kusanagi in the serpent’s tail and presented it to Amaterasu.
claims.statement_id: Dari ekor ular, Susanoo menemukan Kusanagi dan mempersembahkannya kepada Amaterasu.
claims.quote: From within the serpent's tail Susanoo discovered the sword called Kusanagi ("Grass Mower"), and he presented this sword to Amaterasu .

claims.statement: The sword later became one of the three imperial regalia.
claims.statement_id: Pedang itu kemudian menjadi salah satu dari tiga pusaka kekaisaran.
claims.quote: This sword would later become one of the three imperial regalia.

claims.statement: One interpretation reads Orochi as the Hii River and its defeat as taming the river for irrigation.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu tafsir memandang Orochi sebagai Sungai Hii dan kekalahannya sebagai penjinakan sungai untuk irigasi.
claims.quote: The snake Yamata no orochi has been similarly interpreted as the Hii River itself, and the defeat of the snake is thus understood as a description of the taming of the river for irrigation.

claims.statement: Susanoo descended to the headwaters of the Hi River in Izumo Province.
claims.statement_id: Susanoo turun ke hulu Sungai Hi di Provinsi Izumo.
claims.quote: at the headwaters of the Hi River in Izumo Province

claims.statement: Some traditions believed cats could become yōkai as they aged.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian tradisi percaya kucing dapat berubah menjadi yōkai setelah tua.
claims.quote: It was believed that some cats—especially ones with long tails—turned into yokai, or supernatural creatures, at age twelve.

claims.statement: In some accounts, the cat stands on its hind legs and speaks.
claims.statement_id: Dalam sebagian gambaran, kucing itu berdiri dengan kaki belakang dan berbicara.
claims.quote: The cat’s tail would then split into two, the cat would stand erect on its hind legs, and speak.

claims.statement: In some stories bakeneko can assume human form.
claims.statement_id: Dalam sebagian cerita bakeneko dapat mengambil rupa manusia.
claims.quote: In some cases, it would actually assume human form, but all bake-neko were consistent with the idea that animal forms were impermanent

claims.statement: The literal meaning of bake-neko is changed cat.
claims.statement_id: Arti harfiah bake-neko adalah kucing yang berubah.
claims.quote: Indeed, the literal translation of bake-neko, 化け猫, is “changed cat.”

claims.statement: The idea of monstrous cats was especially popular in the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Gagasan kucing menyeramkan populer pada zaman Edo.
claims.quote: The idea of monstrous cats was particularly popular in the Edo Period (1603–1868).

claims.statement: In a Sado Island legend, an old woman becomes a bakeneko and flies to Mount Yahiko.
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda Pulau Sado, seorang perempuan tua menjadi bakeneko dan terbang ke Gunung Yahiko.
claims.quote: One day, when she was rolling around in the sand playing with a cat, she turned into a bakeneko, or monster cat, and flew off toward Mount Yahiko.

claims.statement: The legend’s link to Myōtara-ten is not an official Hōkōin temple tradition.
claims.statement_id: Hubungan legenda itu dengan Myōtara-ten bukan tradisi resmi kuil Hōkōin.
claims.quote: This is not an official tradition, though, and Myōtara-ten worship at Hōkōin temple has no connection with cats.

claims.statement: Bakeneko belong to Japanese supernatural lore.
claims.statement_id: Bakeneko termasuk kisah gaib Jepang.
claims.quote: And in Japan there are bakeneko.

claims.statement: Cats seen standing and licking lantern oil may have inspired fear in the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Kucing yang berdiri dan menjilat minyak lentera mungkin ikut menimbulkan rasa takut pada zaman Edo.
claims.quote: In the Edo period, people used fish oil in lanterns, and the sight of cats standing on their back legs in the dark licking the oil off of lanterns likely caused some fear, as well.

claims.statement: The legend tells of an old woman on Sado Island who loved cats.
claims.statement_id: Legenda itu mengisahkan seorang perempuan tua di Pulau Sado yang menyukai kucing.
claims.quote: there was once an old woman on Sado Island who loved cats.

claims.statement: In the legend people later worshiped the old woman as Myōtara-ten.
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda itu, penduduk kemudian memuja perempuan tua sebagai Myōtara-ten.
claims.quote: In the end, people began worshipping the old woman as Myōtara-ten because the character for cat can be pronounced myō, as well.

claims.statement: In ancient Japan, onryō were spirits of the resentful dead believed to cast curses.
claims.statement_id: Di Jepang kuno, onryō ialah arwah orang yang wafat dengan dendam dan dipercaya dapat mengutuk.
claims.quote: In ancient Japan, the spirits of the dead who died with resentment, called goryō 御霊 or onryō 怨霊, were thought to cast curses.

claims.statement: Onryō were feared as causes of plague and disasters and were pacified.
claims.statement_id: Onryō ditakuti sebagai penyebab wabah dan bencana besar; orang berusaha menenangkan mereka.
claims.quote: Spirits thought to cause plague, natural disaster, or other such large-scale calamities were feared as onryō, and people tried to console and pacify them.

claims.statement: Rites for resentful spirits sought to appease them and avoid curses.
claims.statement_id: Pemujaan roh pendendam bertujuan menenangkan mereka agar kutukan terhindar.
claims.quote: involve the fear of spirits of those who met untimely deaths and attempt to appease them to avoid curses and ensure peace.

claims.statement: Michizane was a scholar and statesman who died in exile.
claims.statement_id: Michizane adalah cendekiawan dan pejabat yang meninggal dalam pengasingan.
claims.quote: Michizane was a distinguished scholar, poet, and statesman who died in exile, having been slandered by enemies at court.

claims.statement: In legend disasters and plagues followed his death; he was pardoned and promoted to appease his spirit, but calamities continued.
claims.statement_id: Menurut legenda, bencana dan wabah mengikuti kematiannya; ia diampuni dan dinaikkan pangkat untuk menenangkan rohnya, namun bencana berlanjut.
claims.quote: After his death, a series of extraordinary natural disasters and plagues caused the untimely deaths of his detractors. In an attempt to appease his vengeful spirit, he was posthumously pardoned and promoted to high office, but the disasters continued.

claims.statement: Michizane was later deified as Tenjin.
claims.statement_id: Michizane kemudian didewakan sebagai Tenjin.
claims.quote: He was deified as Tenjin, an ancient god of agriculture and patron of the falsely accused.

claims.statement: Belief and rites for resentful spirits spread especially from the Heian period onward.
claims.statement_id: Keyakinan dan ritual untuk roh pendendam meluas terutama sejak masa Heian.
claims.quote: However, this form of belief became widespread mainly from the Heian period onward, with rites being widely performed for the spirits of certain individuals

claims.statement: Goryōe rites developed to appease feared spirits.
claims.statement_id: Ritual goryōe dikembangkan untuk menenangkan roh yang ditakuti.
claims.quote: Rituals to appease these spirits, including the goryōe, were developed in tandem.

claims.statement: The account concerns Sugawara Michizane.
claims.statement_id: Kisah ini berhubungan dengan Sugawara Michizane.
claims.quote: dedicated to Sugawara Michizane (845–903). Michizane was a distinguished scholar

claims.statement: In Japanese stories, rokurokubi look like ordinary women but may extend their necks or detach their heads.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah Jepang, rokurokubi tampak seperti perempuan biasa, namun lehernya dapat memanjang atau kepalanya terlepas.
claims.quote: In many Japanese stories, a rokurokubi looks just like an ordinary woman, but her head can go flying off, either at the end of a greatly extended snakelike neck or completely detached from her body

claims.statement: The detached-head form may be called nukekubi.
claims.statement_id: Bentuk dengan kepala terlepas dapat disebut nukekubi.
claims.quote: in which case she may be called a nukekubi

claims.statement: Rokurokubi stories and images became popular in the Edo period amid a wider yōkai boom.
claims.statement_id: Cerita dan seni rokurokubi populer pada zaman Edo bersama meningkatnya minat pada yōkai.
claims.quote: Tales about rokurokubi and depictions in art first became especially popular in the Edo period (1603–1868), when there was a boom of interest in the sometimes frightening, sometimes humorous imaginary creatures known as yōkai.

claims.statement: Rokurokubi are usually shown as women but can also be male.
claims.statement_id: Rokurokubi biasanya digambarkan sebagai perempuan tetapi dapat juga laki-laki.
claims.quote: Incidentally, while rokurokubi are most typically depicted as women, they can also be male.

claims.statement: Hearn’s Rokuro-kubi appeared in Kwaidan in 1904.
claims.statement_id: Cerita Rokuro-kubi karya Hearn muncul dalam Kwaidan tahun 1904.
claims.quote: Hearn’s work: “Rokuro-Kubi”, Kwaidan (1904)

claims.statement: Hearn’s source was Kaibutsu Yoron from 1803.
claims.statement_id: Sumber cerita Hearn berasal dari Kaibutsu Yoron tahun 1803.
claims.quote: Original source: Kaibutsu Yoron Volume 4 (1803)

claims.statement: In this Hearn tale the being’s head separates and flies.
claims.statement_id: Dalam cerita Hearn ini kepala tokohnya terlepas lalu terbang.
claims.quote: However, in this story, the supernatural being is one whose head separates from its body and flies.

claims.statement: Hearn also drew a long-necked rokurokubi in Japanese Goblin Poetry.
claims.statement_id: Hearn juga menggambar rokurokubi berleher panjang dalam Japanese Goblin Poetry.
claims.quote: Hearn’s humourous drawing of the “rokurokubi” with its elongated neck appears in Japanese Goblin Poetry.

claims.statement: In Kwaidan, the priest sees headless bodies and flying heads at night.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Kwaidan, pendeta melihat tubuh tanpa kepala dan kepala beterbangan pada malam hari.
claims.quote: In the middle of the night, he discovers their headless bodies in one room and the heads flying around outside, planning to eat him.

claims.statement: Ebisu is a god of good catches and guardian of fisheries.
claims.statement_id: Ebisu adalah dewa hasil tangkapan dan pelindung perikanan.
claims.quote: Ebisu is the god of good catches and is worshipped as a guardian deity of fisheries.

claims.statement: Ebisu is one of Japan’s Seven Gods of Fortune.
claims.statement_id: Ebisu termasuk tujuh dewa keberuntungan Jepang.
claims.quote: Ebisu, one of Japan’s Seven Gods of Fortune.

claims.statement: Ebisu is a kami commonly pictured with a fishing pole or sea bream.
claims.statement_id: Ebisu sebagai kami lazim digambarkan dengan pancing atau ikan tai.
claims.quote: The opulent image of this kami holding a fishing pole or a sea bream is known intimately by people throughout Japan.

claims.statement: Fishers thank Ebisu after a large catch and pray for good fishing after a poor catch.
claims.statement_id: Nelayan berterima kasih kepada Ebisu setelah hasil besar dan berdoa setelah hasil sedikit.
claims.quote: Fishermen give thanks to Ebisu after a large catch, and pray for a bountiful catch after a poor one.

claims.statement: Ebisu is also regarded as a guardian of commerce.
claims.statement_id: Ebisu juga dianggap pelindung perdagangan.
claims.quote: Ebisu also possesses characteristics as a tutelary of commerce

claims.statement: Villagers pray to Village Ebisu in Isso for business success.
claims.statement_id: Warga memohon keberhasilan usaha kepada Ebisu Desa di Isso.
claims.quote: Villagers pray to this Ebisu for success in business.

claims.statement: A Mugio statue holds a skipjack rather than the usual sea bream.
claims.statement_id: Patung Ebisu di Mugio membawa cakalang, berbeda dari gambaran lazim dengan ikan tai.
claims.quote: Ebisu usually holds a sea bream, but this one holds a skipjack

claims.statement: An Ebisu festival each January 10 prays for safety at sea and good catches.
claims.statement_id: Pesta Ebisu setiap 10 Januari memohon keselamatan di laut dan hasil tangkapan baik.
claims.quote: A festival is held every January 10 to thank this Ebisu for his blessings and protection, and to pray for safety at sea as well as good fishing.

claims.statement: A wooden Ebisu statue in Isso is worshiped as Village Ebisu.
claims.statement_id: Di Isso ada patung kayu yang dipuja sebagai Ebisu Desa.
claims.quote: Another Ebisu statue in Isso is made of yakusugi cedar and worshipped at a small stone altar known as the “Village Ebisu.”

claims.statement: A wooden Ebisu statue stands at Mugio harbor.
claims.statement_id: Patung kayu Ebisu berada di Pelabuhan Mugio.
claims.quote: A wooden carved Ebisu looks out over the port of Mugio on the southeastern coast of the island.

claims.statement: These practices take place on Yakushima.
claims.statement_id: Lokasi praktik ini berada di Yakushima.
claims.quote: Yakushima, a mountainous island on the Kuroshio Current with limited arable land

claims.statement: Japanese dragon images blend Chinese dragons, Buddhist nāga, and local water-deity ideas.
claims.statement_id: Gambaran naga Jepang memadukan pengaruh naga Tiongkok, nāga Buddha, dan pandangan setempat tentang dewa air.
claims.quote: Japanese images of dragons are a blend of three influences: China’s mythical dragon, the nāga of Hindu myth and Buddhist scripture, and native Japanese views of it as a water deity.

claims.statement: In Japan dragons are called ryū and revered as Buddhist protectors.
claims.statement_id: Di Jepang naga disebut ryū dan dihormati sebagai pelindung dalam tradisi Buddha.
claims.quote: In Japan, the dragon, or ryū, looks like a Chinese dragon, but is venerated like the nāga as a protector of Buddhism.

claims.statement: Dragons are linked to rain and believed to dwell in seas or other waters.
claims.statement_id: Naga dikaitkan dengan hujan dan dipercaya mendiami laut atau perairan lain.
claims.quote: Dragons are associated with rain and have long been tied to folk beliefs about water, the creatures often being said to reside in the ocean or other bodies of water.

claims.statement: At many shrines dragons are revered for rain, flood protection, health, and luck.
claims.statement_id: Di banyak kuil naga dipuja untuk hujan, perlindungan banjir, kesehatan, dan keberuntungan.
claims.quote: Dragons themselves are objects of worship at many shrines, where they are venerated for reasons like bringing rain, stopping floods, and ensuring health, long life, and luck.

claims.statement: Kanō Tan’yū’s painting draws on dragons’ symbolism as masters of cloud and rain.
claims.statement_id: Lukisan Kanō Tan’yū menampilkan naga sebagai penguasa awan dan hujan.
claims.quote: These near-experimental visual effects, achieved through bold manipulation of the fluid medium, align with the traditional symbolism of dragons as masters of cloud and rain.

claims.statement: Ink washes in a painting of paired dragons suggest rain through clouds.
claims.statement_id: Sapuan tinta pada lukisan sepasang naga menimbulkan kesan hujan di tengah awan.
claims.quote: This pair of dragons is painted with extensive water washes, visible in the flowing marks where diluted black ink bleeds across the silk surface and creates the impression of rain falling through layered clouds.

claims.statement: A Japanese mandala shows dragon kings in a watery world and was used in rites to end drought.
claims.statement_id: Mandala Jepang menampilkan raja naga dalam dunia air dan dipakai dalam ritual mengakhiri kekeringan.
claims.quote: This unusual mandala, a sketch from a compendium of esoteric Buddhist images, set in the watery world of dragon kings, was used in rites to end drought.

claims.statement: Daija is a guardian dragon venerated at a shrine by Ōnuma Pond.
claims.statement_id: Daija adalah naga penjaga yang dipuja di kuil dekat Kolam Ōnuma.
claims.quote: The red torii gate visible on the shore belongs to Daija-jinjya Shrine, dedicated to Daija, a dragon seen in this area as a guardian spirit.

claims.statement: In one local legend Daija could transform into a man.
claims.statement_id: Dalam satu versi legenda setempat, Daija dapat berubah menjadi manusia.
claims.quote: According to one version of a local legend, every spring Daija used to transform into a man and go to see the cherry blossoms in the mountains.

claims.statement: The legend says Daija summoned a storm that flooded the area.
claims.statement_id: Legenda itu menyebut Daija memanggil badai yang membanjiri wilayah itu.
claims.quote: Enraged, Daija summoned a great storm to flood the region.

claims.statement: Dragon images adorn ritual wash basins and shrine buildings.
claims.statement_id: Gambar naga menghiasi tempat pembasuhan tangan dan bangunan kuil.
claims.quote: They frequently appear as decorative elements on temizuya basins for ritually washing hands or as carvings or paintings to protect shrine buildings from fire.

claims.statement: In Japanese folklore, kodama are tree spirits believed to give trees personality.
claims.statement_id: Dalam cerita rakyat Jepang, kodama adalah roh pohon yang dipercaya memberi pohon suatu kepribadian.
claims.quote: These tree spirits are known as kodama, and according to Japanese folklore, the kodama give the tree a personality.

claims.statement: Tree spirits are associated with trees that have reached a hundred years of age.
claims.statement_id: Roh pohon dikaitkan dengan pohon yang telah berusia seratus tahun.
claims.quote: which holds that spirits inhabit trees that reach one hundred years of age.

claims.statement: Venerated old trees could be marked with sacred shimenawa rope.
claims.statement_id: Pohon tua yang dihormati dapat ditandai dengan tali suci shimenawa.
claims.quote: In fact, they were marked with a sacred rope called a shimenawa

claims.statement: Cutting such a tree was believed to bring an angry spirit.
claims.statement_id: Menebang pohon semacam itu dipercaya dapat membangkitkan roh yang marah.
claims.quote: if anyone chopped down the tree, they would have to deal with an angry spirit.

claims.statement: A Japanese artwork presents kodama as unseen forest spirits.
claims.statement_id: Sebuah karya seni di Jepang menggambarkan kodama sebagai roh hutan yang tidak terlihat.
claims.quote: KODAMA are the tree spirits that live in the forest. They are invisible to human eyes

claims.statement: The artwork connects the name kodama with echoes of voices in the forest.
claims.statement_id: Karya seni tersebut menghubungkan nama kodama dengan gema suara dalam hutan.
claims.quote: Next, visitors hear the echo (also pronounced kodama in Japanese) of the voices in the forest even though there is no one there.

claims.statement: In an Engishiki liturgy, a particular tree kami is called a kodama.
claims.statement_id: Dalam liturgi Engishiki, satu kami pohon disebut kodama.
claims.quote: the former is described as a kodama (tree spirit), while the latter is called an inadama.

claims.statement: Namazu is a mythical fish said to lie beneath Japan and cause earthquakes.
claims.statement_id: Namazu adalah ikan mitos yang menurut legenda berada di bawah kepulauan Jepang dan menyebabkan gempa.
claims.quote: This catfish represents the namazu: a mythical fish that, according to legend, lies under the islands of Japan and causes earthquakes.

claims.statement: Japanese legend attributes earthquakes to the movements of a giant catfish below Japan.
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda Jepang, gerakan lele raksasa di bawah Jepang dipercaya menyebabkan gempa.
claims.quote: According to Japanese legend, earthquakes were caused by the movements of a monster catfish that lived under the island of Japan.

claims.statement: One print depicts Namazu beneath a great stone of Kashima Shrine.
claims.statement_id: Satu cetakan menggambarkan Namazu di bawah batu besar Kuil Kashima.
claims.quote: Here the monster Namazu (is lifting up the great stone of the Kashima Shrine by which it has been fixed under the ground for a long time.

claims.statement: Belief in the huge underground catfish Ōnamazu was widespread in the Edo period.
claims.statement_id: Pada zaman Edo keyakinan tentang lele besar Ōnamazu di bawah Jepang tersebar luas.
claims.quote: During the Edo era, a belief became widespread in mainstream society that a huge catfish called Ohnamazu lived in the mud, under the islands of Japan, and was the cause of earthquakes.

claims.statement: Namazu-e prints mainly appeared after the Ansei Edo earthquake of November 11, 1855.
claims.statement_id: Cetakan namazu-e terutama muncul setelah gempa Ansei Edo pada 11 November 1855.
claims.quote: The term generally refers to prints published after the Ansei Edo earthquake, which struck Edo on the night of the 2nd day of the 10th month of Ansei 2 (November 11, 1855).

claims.statement: Namazu-e often anthropomorphize the fish and show gods, craftsmen, and stones.
claims.statement_id: Cetakan namazu-e sering memanusiakan lele dan menampilkan dewa, pengrajin, serta batu.
claims.quote: Many works anthropomorphize the catfish, and recurring motifs include oni (demons), Ebisu, Daikokuten, craftsmen, foundation stone, gourds, sacred horses, and Kashima Daimyojin.

claims.statement: Some prints depict gods and townspeople punishing the catfish.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian gambar menunjukkan lele dihukum oleh dewa dan penduduk kota.
claims.quote: These paintings often show images of catfish being scolded and attacked by gods and townspeople, or eaten as kabayaki

claims.statement: Prints also show people who profited from rebuilding after the earthquake.
claims.statement_id: Gambar juga menampilkan orang yang mendapat penghasilan dari pemulihan setelah gempa.
claims.quote: People who profited from the post-disaster restoration, such as carpenters, plasterers, lumber traders, firefighters, and kawaraban (newspaper) sellers who distributed flash reports about the earthquake, were often drawn into the Ukiyo-e pictures.

claims.statement: The prints formed part of local responses to the disaster.
claims.statement_id: Cetakan tersebut menjadi bagian dari tanggapan penduduk terhadap bencana.
claims.quote: These imaginative and sometimes brutal depictions served as a unique source of information and reassurance to the local population.

claims.statement: Nekomata are Japanese yōkai said to transform from old or large cats.
claims.statement_id: Nekomata adalah yōkai Jepang yang menurut cerita berasal dari kucing tua atau besar.
claims.quote: Nekomata (ねこまた) are Japanese yōkai said to have transformed from old and large cats.

claims.statement: Nekomata tails are depicted as splitting in two.
claims.statement_id: Ekor nekomata digambarkan terbelah menjadi dua.
claims.quote: their tails split down the middle into two identical tails.

claims.statement: Nekomata are said to speak, walk on their hind legs, and cause mischief.
claims.statement_id: Nekomata dikisahkan dapat berbicara, berjalan pada kaki belakang, dan mengganggu orang.
claims.quote: speaking human languages as well as walking on their rear legs, causing mischief.

claims.statement: Some stories describe nekomata as mountain beasts that attack people.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian kisah menyebut nekomata sebagai makhluk gunung yang menyerang manusia.
claims.quote: Some believe it is a mountain beast, and it is known to sometimes attack humans.

claims.statement: Toriyama Sekien’s art depicts nekomata dancing on two legs.
claims.statement_id: Seni Toriyama Sekien menggambarkan nekomata menari dengan dua kaki.
claims.quote: One sign of this, evidently, was dancing madly on two legs—this is how the nekomata is depicted in Toriyama Sekien’s Gazu hyakki yagyō

claims.statement: The distinction between bakeneko and nekomata is often unclear.
claims.statement_id: Perbedaan bakeneko dan nekomata dalam sumber seni sering tidak jelas.
claims.quote: While the distinction between bakeneko and nekomata is seldom clear

claims.statement: A Nakanomata tale says Ushiki Kichijūrō defeated a nekomata.
claims.statement_id: Kisah Nakanomata menuturkan Ushiki Kichijūrō mengalahkan nekomata.
claims.quote: In the village of Nakanomata in Niigata Prefecture, there is a famous story about a strong villager, Ushiki Kichijūrō, who was able to defeat a feline yōkai called nekomata.

claims.statement: A nekomata legend is associated with Mount Nekomata in Toyama.
claims.statement_id: Ada legenda tentang nekomata di Gunung Nekomata, Toyama.
claims.quote: There is a legend connected to Mount Nekomata in Toyama Prefecture’s Kurobe gorge.

claims.statement: In that mountain legend, the creature preys on local people.
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda Gunung Nekomata, makhluk itu memangsa penduduk setempat.
claims.quote: It began causing trouble, even eating the local people.

claims.statement: Ninigi is a kami and grandchild of Amaterasu who descends from heaven.
claims.statement_id: Ninigi adalah kami cucu Amaterasu yang turun dari langit.
claims.quote: The kami who, as grandchild of Amaterasu ōmikami, descended

claims.statement: Ninigi descends from Takamanohara to Takachiho to rule the earthly land.
claims.statement_id: Ninigi turun dari Takamanohara ke Takachiho untuk memerintah negeri di bumi.
claims.quote: from the Plain of High Heaven (Takamanohara) to the peak of Takachiho in Hyūga of Tsukushi (present-day Kyushu) to rule over the "Central Land of Reed Plains"

claims.statement: Ninigi’s father Oshihomimi was first commanded to descend and rule.
claims.statement_id: Oshihomimi, ayah Ninigi, semula ditugaskan turun dan memerintah.
claims.quote: Ninigi's father Oshihomimi was first commanded to descend and rule the Central Land of Reed Plains

claims.statement: Ninigi descended in his father’s place.
claims.statement_id: Ninigi turun menggantikan ayahnya.
claims.quote: Ninigi descended in place of his father Oshihomimi.

claims.statement: Amaterasu and Takamimusuhi supplied five attendant kami and the sword, mirror, and jewel.
claims.statement_id: Amaterasu dan Takamimusuhi membekali Ninigi dengan lima kami pengiring serta pedang, cermin, dan permata.
claims.quote: Furnished by Amaterasu and Takamimusuhi with five retainer kami, as well as with the symbolic sword, mirror and jewel

claims.statement: One account places Ninigi’s descent at Kushifurutake in Takachiho.
claims.statement_id: Satu kisah menempatkan turunnya rombongan Ninigi di Kushifurutake, Takachiho.
claims.quote: It is written that Ninigi and his procession made their way through the heavens and descended at “Kushifurutake of Takachiho.”

claims.statement: Ninigi’s three treasures later became Japan’s imperial regalia.
claims.statement_id: Tiga pusaka Ninigi kemudian menjadi regalia kekaisaran Jepang.
claims.quote: These three treasures would later become the Imperial Regalia of Japan.

claims.statement: Kushifuru Shrine was built in 1694 on the mountain believed to mark Ninigi’s arrival.
claims.statement_id: Kuil Kushifuru dibangun pada 1694 di gunung yang dipercaya sebagai tempat kedatangan Ninigi.
claims.quote: Kushifuru Shine, which venerates Ninigi, was built in 1694 upon the mountain where he and his procession are believed to have arrived.

claims.statement: In a local legend Ninigi scatters rice and the fog lifts.
claims.statement_id: Dalam legenda setempat, Ninigi menaburkan padi dan kabut penghalang terangkat.
claims.quote: They urged Ninigi to take rice from the stalks he held in his hand and scatter it over the land. Upon doing so, the fog lifted

claims.statement: In Japanese mythology Ninigi’s great-grandson becomes the first emperor.
claims.statement_id: Dalam mitologi Jepang, cicit Ninigi menjadi kaisar pertama.
claims.quote: In Japanese mythology, Ninigi’s great-grandson becomes the first emperor of Japan

claims.statement: Tsukumogami are animate household objects.
claims.statement_id: Tsukumogami adalah benda rumah tangga yang hidup.
claims.quote: Tsukumogami are animate household objects.

claims.statement: In the Muromachi tale Tsukumogami ki, containers, tools, and instruments receive souls after nearly one hundred years.
claims.statement_id: Dalam Tsukumogami ki zaman Muromachi, wadah, alat, dan instrumen menerima jiwa setelah dipakai hampir seratus tahun.
claims.quote: An otogizōshi (“companion tale”) titled Tsukumogami ki (“Record of tool specters”; Muromachi period) explains that after a service life of nearly one hundred years, utsuwamono or kibutsu (containers, tools, and instruments) receive souls.

claims.statement: Folktales describe tsukumogami as tools and other objects that acquire spirits over time.
claims.statement_id: Cerita rakyat menyebut tsukumogami sebagai alat dan benda yang memperoleh roh setelah lama digunakan.
claims.quote: Folktales tell of tsukumogami, tools and other objects that acquire a spirit after a number of years have passed.

claims.statement: An object may become a malicious yōkai or benevolent spirit depending on its treatment.
claims.statement_id: Benda itu dapat berubah menjadi yōkai jahat atau roh baik menurut perlakuan manusia.
claims.quote: An item becomes a tsukumogami after a hundred years, and depending on how it has been treated, it might transform into a malicious yōkai or a benevolent spirit.

claims.statement: A scholar argues that Tsukumogami ki spread Shingon Buddhist teachings.
claims.statement_id: Peneliti menilai Tsukumogami ki dipakai untuk menyebarkan ajaran Buddha Shingon.
claims.quote: the principal motivation of the author(s) in writing it was to spread the doctrines of Shingon Esoteric Buddhism

claims.statement: Night-parade scrolls show tsukumogami as living objects with limbs.
claims.statement_id: Gulungan arak-arakan malam menampilkan tsukumogami sebagai benda hidup yang memiliki anggota badan.
claims.quote: many of the monsters that populate these scrolls are tsukumogami 付喪神, everyday objects that have gained sentience, sprouted limbs, and taken to frolicking with the demons.

claims.statement: Prints show animated cups, teapots, ladles, a shamisen, fans, and mochi tools.
claims.statement_id: Gambar menampilkan cangkir, teko, sendok, shamisen, kipas, lesung, dan alu yang hidup.
claims.quote: a pair of teacups that together make a set of eyes; a teapot with legs and face; a ladle; a kettle; a shamisen 三味線 holding a plectrum and a songbook; a folding fan wielding itself; and a large mortar and pestle

claims.statement: The depicted animated objects were familiar items of everyday life.
claims.statement_id: Benda yang hidup dalam gambar merupakan peralatan sehari-hari.
claims.quote: the objects that have become animated are ones that an early modern viewer would still have been familiar with from everyday life.

claims.statement: One furry-legged kettle is a disguised tanuki, not a tsukumogami.
claims.statement_id: Salah satu teko berkaki berbulu adalah tanuki yang berubah rupa, bukan tsukumogami.
claims.quote: the kettle’s legs are furry and it has a tail, too; this tells us that it’s not a tsukumogami proper, but a shape-shifting tanuki

claims.statement: In Japanese folklore, tsukumogami are tools or household objects that acquire a spirit.
claims.statement_id: Dalam cerita rakyat Jepang, tsukumogami adalah alat atau benda rumah tangga yang memperoleh roh.
claims.quote: In Japanese folklore, tools or household objects that have acquired a kami or spirit.

claims.statement: Yama-uba, also known as yamamba, is a Japanese yōkai.
claims.statement_id: Yama-uba atau yamamba adalah yōkai Jepang.
claims.quote: Yamamba (山むば) is a Japanese yōkai also known as yamauba (山うば)

claims.statement: Yama-uba are female yōkai living in mountain huts.
claims.statement_id: Yama-uba adalah yōkai perempuan yang tinggal di pondok gunung.
claims.quote: Yamamba are female yōkai that live alone in mountain huts.

claims.statement: In some tales she offers lodging as an old or young woman.
claims.statement_id: Dalam beberapa cerita ia menawarkan tempat bermalam sebagai perempuan tua atau muda.
claims.quote: They occasionally offer a place to sleep for the night to travelers in the form of an old woman or beautiful young woman.

claims.statement: Some stories have yama-uba reward those who treat her kindly.
claims.statement_id: Ada kisah yama-uba yang memberi keberuntungan kepada orang yang baik padanya.
claims.quote: tales in which yamamba is a benevolent yōkai that gives good fortune to people who were kind to her.

claims.statement: Rosetsu’s painting shows a fearsome yama-uba with her adopted child.
claims.statement_id: Lukisan Rosetsu menggambarkan yama-uba yang menakutkan bersama anak angkatnya.
claims.quote: This painting by the Kyoto-based artist Nagasawa Rosetsu (1754–1799) portrays a fearsome-looking yamauba (“mountain witch”) and her adoptive child.

claims.statement: Legend says yama-uba raised the superhumanly strong Kintarō on a mountain in Hakone.
claims.statement_id: Legenda menyebut yama-uba membesarkan Kintarō di Gunung Hakone; anak itu sangat kuat.
claims.quote: Raised by the yamauba on a mountain in Hakone (just south of Tokyo), Kintaro was a child with superhuman strength who fought monsters and demons from an early age.

claims.statement: The painting was donated to Itsukushima Shrine in 1797.
claims.statement_id: Lukisan itu disumbangkan ke Kuil Itsukushima pada 1797.
claims.quote: the painting was donated to Itsukushima Shrine in 1797 by a group of wealthy merchants from Hiroshima

claims.statement: Yama-uba appears as a character in a Noh drama.
claims.statement_id: Tokoh yama-uba muncul dalam drama Noh.
claims.quote: A similar character appears in the Noh drama of the same name YAMAUBA

claims.statement: Yama-uba is often pictured with disheveled hair and ragged clothes.
claims.statement_id: Yama-uba sering digambar dengan rambut terurai dan pakaian compang-camping.
claims.quote: Yamauba is usually represented with long hair hanging down in dishevelled tresses, and dressed in tattered, flimsy clothing.

claims.statement: Utamaro also depicted yama-uba as beautiful women.
claims.statement_id: Utamaro juga menggambar yama-uba sebagai perempuan cantik.
claims.quote: (1754-1806) portrayed many Yamauba in the guise of beautiful women

claims.statement: In some stories yama-uba transforms and eats sleeping guests.
claims.statement_id: Setelah tamu tertidur, yama-uba dalam kisah menampakkan wujudnya dan memakan tamu.
claims.quote: After their guests fall asleep, they transform into their true form and eat their guests.

claims.statement: Yama-uba stories often have her prey on travelers and merchants.
claims.statement_id: Kisah yama-uba sering menyebutnya memangsa pelancong dan pedagang.
claims.quote: yamamba typically preys on travelers and merchants such as ox-drivers, horse drivers, and coopers

claims.statement: Amabie is a yōkai in Japanese folklore.
claims.statement_id: Amabie adalah yōkai dalam cerita rakyat Jepang.
claims.quote: Amabie (アマビエ) is one of yōkai (妖怪), a class of mythological and supernatural spirits or monsters in Japanese folklore.

claims.statement: The 1846 story places Amabie in Higo, now Kumamoto.
claims.statement_id: Kisah tahun 1846 menempatkan kemunculan Amabie di Higo, Kumamoto kini.
claims.quote: It is said to have appeared in Higo no kuni, today’s Kumamoto prefecture, in 1846

claims.statement: The early story describes a recurring light in the sea off Higo.
claims.statement_id: Dalam kisah awal, cahaya tampak tiap malam di laut Higo.
claims.quote: A glowing object appeared every night in the sea of Higo Province [today’s Kumamoto prefecture].

claims.statement: Amabie says it lives in the sea, predicts harvest and disease, and asks that its image be shown.
claims.statement_id: Amabie mengaku hidup di laut, meramalkan panen baik dan penyakit, serta meminta rupanya digambar dan ditunjukkan.
claims.quote: I live in the sea. My name is Amabié. Good harvest will continue for six years. At the same time disease will spread. Draw me and show me to the people as soon as possible.

claims.statement: A town official investigated and encountered the creature.
claims.statement_id: Seorang pejabat kota pergi menyelidiki dan menemui makhluk itu.
claims.quote: When the town’s official went there and found something like the drawing, he was told

claims.statement: The Amabie story spread through woodblock kawaraban bulletins.
claims.statement_id: Kisah Amabie disebarkan melalui lembar berita bergambar kawaraban.
claims.quote: the story was printed and disseminated in kawaraban (woodblock-printed bulletins that were a kind of newspaper of the time featuring news, outrageous gossip, and rumors).

claims.statement: During COVID-19 people shared Amabie drawings and other creations online.
claims.statement_id: Pada pandemi COVID-19 orang membagikan gambar dan kreasi Amabie melalui media sosial.
claims.quote: A lot of people responded by posting images of illustrations, manga, stuffed toys and other figures of Amabie with #アマビエチャレンジ

claims.statement: Japan’s health ministry used Amabie in pandemic awareness messages.
claims.statement_id: Kementerian kesehatan Jepang memakai Amabie untuk pesan kesadaran pandemi.
claims.quote: Japan’s Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare even adapted Amabie as a mascot to warn people about the pandemic.

claims.statement: A Tokyo museum also records the 1846 Higo sea story and disease prophecy.
claims.statement_id: Museum Tokyo juga mencatat Amabie muncul dalam kisah 1846 di laut Higo dan meramalkan penyakit.
claims.quote: in 1846 (Koka 3), Amabie was spotted in the sea in Higo Province. The record says that the two creatures predicted the spread of disease and conveyed how to avoid it.

claims.statement: Hoori is another name of the kami Hohodemi.
claims.statement_id: Hoori adalah nama lain kami Hohodemi.
claims.quote: Hoori no mikoto(Kojiki, Nihongi)

claims.statement: Hoori is the child of Ninigi and Konohana Sakuyahime and a hunter called Yamasachihiko.
claims.statement_id: Hoori adalah anak Ninigi dan Konohana Sakuyahime yang dikenal sebagai pemburu Yamasachihiko.
claims.quote: Offspring of Ninigi and Konohana Sakuyahime. Called Yamasachihiko ("mountain-gift-man") for his unique success in the hunt

claims.statement: Yamasachihiko is a skilled hunter and Umisachihiko an expert fisher.
claims.statement_id: Yamasachihiko mahir berburu, sedangkan saudaranya Umisachihiko mahir memancing.
claims.quote: Yamasachi-hiko, who grows up to be a master hunter, and Umisachi-hiko, who becomes an expert fisherman.

claims.statement: Hoori loses the fishing hook borrowed from his brother.
claims.statement_id: Hoori kehilangan kail pinjaman saudaranya.
claims.quote: Yamasachi-hiko loses the hook he has borrowed and cannot find it, no matter how hard he tries.

claims.statement: Shiotsuchi sends Hoori to the sea god’s palace.
claims.statement_id: Shiotsuchi menyuruh Hoori mencari kail di istana dewa laut.
claims.quote: The despairing Yamasachi-hiko is visited by an old man named Shiotsuchi, who tells him to board a boat and search at the palace of Wadatsumi, god of the sea.

claims.statement: Hoori marries Toyotama and stays with her for three years.
claims.statement_id: Hoori menikahi Toyotama dan tinggal bersamanya selama tiga tahun.
claims.quote: Yamasachi-hiko is invited to a grand feast and eventually marries Toyotama. The two live together happily for three years.

claims.statement: The lost hook is found stuck in a sea bream.
claims.statement_id: Kail yang hilang ditemukan tersangkut pada ikan tai.
claims.quote: Wadatsumi calls for the sea bream, whose pain is found to be caused by a stuck fishing hook that Yamasachi-hiko recognizes to be his brother's.

claims.statement: Hoori receives jewels to raise and lower the tide.
claims.statement_id: Hoori menerima permata pengangkat dan penurun pasang laut.
claims.quote: a "tide-raising jewel" and "tide-lowering jewel."

claims.statement: Hoori uses tide jewels in a renewed conflict with his brother.
claims.statement_id: Hoori memakai permata pasang saat menghadapi saudaranya lagi.
claims.quote: Yamasachi-hiko uses the orbs given to him by the god of the sea and calls in the tide, almost drowning Umisachi-hiko, who finally relents.

claims.statement: An Aoshima Shrine winter festival reenacts Hoori’s return and a purification in the sea.
claims.statement_id: Pesta musim dingin di Kuil Aoshima memperagakan kepulangan Hoori dan ritual penyucian di laut.
claims.quote: an annual winter festival reenacts the scene of Yamasachi-hiko’s return from the sea god’s palace and his welcoming at shore by a delighted crowd. Participants wearing only loincloths rush into the cold waves to greet the deity and undertake a ritual purification.
