claims.statement: Tanuki are raccoon dogs believed in folklore to change form and trick humans.
claims.statement_id: Tanuki adalah anjing rakun yang dalam folklor dipercaya dapat berubah rupa dan mempermainkan manusia.
claims.quote: animals such as foxes and tanuki (raccoon dogs) were long believed to possess the ability to change form to trick humans

claims.statement: The folklore tanuki is celebrated for transformation and mischief.
claims.statement_id: Tanuki dalam folklor terkenal karena perubahan wujud dan keusilan.
claims.quote: The tanuki, a raccoon dog from Japanese folklore, is celebrated for its powers of transformation and mischievous humor.

claims.statement: Shapeshifting tanuki belong to the bakemono or yōkai tradition.
claims.statement_id: Tanuki yang berubah rupa termasuk tradisi bakemono atau yōkai.
claims.quote: Back in the Edo period, yōkai were known as bakemono—shape-shifters.

claims.statement: Bunbuku chagama tells of a tanuki turning into a teakettle.
claims.statement_id: Bunbuku chagama mengisahkan tanuki berubah menjadi ketel teh.
claims.quote: One of the most popular tanuki stories (Bunbuku chagama, or “The Lucky Teakettle”) involves a tanuki who turned himself into a teakettle.

claims.statement: In many versions the tanuki’s tail and legs appear when the kettle is heated.
claims.statement_id: Dalam banyak versi, ekor dan kaki tanuki muncul saat ketel dipanaskan.
claims.quote: most at some point involve the tanuki losing his concentration when placed over hot coals, so that his tail and legs pop out of the teakettle.

claims.statement: Some versions associate the tale with Morinji temple in Gunma.
claims.statement_id: Sebagian versi menempatkan kisah itu di Kuil Morinji, Gunma.
claims.quote: Some version of the story associate it with the temple of Morinji in Gunma

claims.statement: A yōkai game print depicts a belly-drumming tanuki.
claims.statement_id: Gambar permainan yōkai menampilkan tanuki memukul perutnya seperti genderang.
claims.quote: The “belly-drum” (haratsuzumi) is, of course, a tanuki happily doing his thing.

claims.statement: Another picture shows a tanuki halfway transformed into Tofu Boy.
claims.statement_id: Gambar lain memperlihatkan tanuki setengah berubah menjadi Bocah Tahu.
claims.quote: What we have here is a tanuki that has half shape-shifted into Tofu Boy—a yōkai pretending to be another yōkai.

claims.statement: Furry legs and a tail reveal the disguised tanuki.
claims.statement_id: Kaki berbulu dan ekor dalam gambar mengungkap penyamaran tanuki.
claims.quote: but then we notice the furry legs and tail.

claims.statement: Ukemochi is a deity in an alternative Nihongi account.
claims.statement_id: Ukemochi adalah dewa yang muncul dalam versi alternatif Nihongi.
claims.quote: A deity appearing in an "alternate writing" quoted within Nihongi.

claims.statement: Uke and uka mean food; Ukemochi is a tutelary of foodstuffs.
claims.statement_id: Uke dan uka berarti makanan; nama Ukemochi menunjuk pada pelindung pangan.
claims.quote: The name uke is synonymous with uka, meaning "food," with the result that ukemochi no kami means a tutelary of foodstuffs

claims.statement: Amaterasu directs Tsukuyomi to visit Ukemochi.
claims.statement_id: Amaterasu menyuruh Tsukuyomi menemui Ukemochi.
claims.quote: Amaterasu commanded Tsukuyomi to go to Ukemochi

claims.statement: Ukemochi produces various foods from her mouth.
claims.statement_id: Ukemochi mengeluarkan aneka makanan dari mulutnya.
claims.quote: Ukemochi produced various foods from her mouth, including "things broad of fin" and "things narrow of fin," "things rough of hair" and "things soft of hair,"

claims.statement: Tsukuyomi kills Ukemochi because he regards her food as polluted.
claims.statement_id: Tsukuyomi marah karena menganggap makanan itu tercemar, lalu membunuh Ukemochi.
claims.quote: Tsukuyomi, however, was enraged at being served foods that were "polluted" (since they had issued from Ukemochi's mouth), and drew his sword and killed Ukemochi.

claims.statement: Cattle, horses, rice, wheat, and beans emerge from Ukemochi’s body.
claims.statement_id: Dari jenazah Ukemochi muncul sapi, kuda, padi, gandum, dan kacang.
claims.quote: cattle and horses were produced from the head of Ukemochi's dead body, rice was produced from her belly, and wheat and beans were produced from her genitals.

claims.statement: Amaterasu plants the grains and seeds in a food-origin myth.
claims.statement_id: Amaterasu menanam biji-bijian itu; kisahnya menjelaskan asal makanan.
claims.quote: Amaterasu planted the various grains and seeds in fields and paddies, a story said to represent one type of food-origin myth.

claims.statement: The Kojiki tells a related tale about Susanoo and the food deity Ōgetsuhime.
claims.statement_id: Kojiki menuturkan kisah sejenis tentang Susanoo dan dewi pangan Ōgetsuhime.
claims.quote: The mythic origin of food is written in the Kojiki (Records of Ancient Matters). Once upon a time, Susanoo, one of the gods of Japan, asked Ogetsuhime, a goddesses, to give him food.

claims.statement: The Nihon-shoki tells of Tsukuyomi killing Ukemochi.
claims.statement_id: Nihon-shoki menuturkan Tsukuyomi membunuh dewi Ukemochi.
claims.quote: The Nihon-shoki (Chronicles of Japan) has a similar myth in which Tsukuyomi, the god of the moon, murders Ukemochi, a goddess.

claims.statement: Amaterasu shuns Tsukuyomi, explaining the alternating sun and moon.
claims.statement_id: Amaterasu menjauhi Tsukuyomi; kisah itu menjelaskan pergantian matahari dan bulan.
claims.quote: Amaterasu, the goddess of the sun, who dispatched Tsukuyomi to Ukemochi, became furious about the murder and said she no longer wanted to stay in the same broad sky with him. This is explained as the origin of the alternative appearances of the sun and the moon in the sky.
